content: Our correspondent Wassim Cornet reports from a Democratic watch party in Los Angeles where "people are opening bottles of champagne" following the Democrats' first victories in these midterm elections. We also speak with France 24's Jessica Le Masurier, reporting from Detroit, Michigan.
summary: Wassim Cornet reported from a Democratic watch party in Los Angeles where people opened champagne bottles after the Democrats' first victories in the midterm elections. The coverage also featured France 24's Jessica Le Masurier reporting from Detroit, Michigan.

content: Democrats, once viewing the political map as an almost impossible lift, now say a Senate majority may be within reach, even as their path cuts through several conservative states. content: California polls have just closed, but the state’s vote‑counting process is expected to take longer than usual. The article explores the reasons behind California’s slower tallying, featuring a discussion with Guy Marzorati, political correspondent at KQED in the Bay Area.
summary: California polls have just closed and results are expected to take longer to be reported. The delay is discussed with guest Guy Marzorati, political correspondent at KQED in the Bay Area.

title: House Minority Leader Hakeen Jeffries vows to target corruption after expected majority
content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told supporters on Tuesday that he intends to use the expected Democratic majority in the House to pursue corruption. He said, “We’re going to bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country,” noting that allegations of grift by President Donald Trump have dominated voters’ concerns in the midterm election.

Jeffries, who is on track to become speaker of the House in the new Congress, framed the initiative as a response to the corruption narrative that has shaped the campaign.
summary: The top Democrat in the US House of Representatives said on Tuesday he will use his expected majority to go after corruption. House Minority Leader Hakeen Jeffries, who is on track to become speaker of the House in the new Congress, told supporters they will bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption.
author: France 24

title: Bomb threats target multiple flights to Warsaw, Rome, Sofia and other European cities
content: Multiple flights to European airports were subject to bomb threats. The threats involved two passenger planes bound for Warsaw, a Ryanair flight from London to Spain, two flights to Rome, and a flight from Israel to Sofia. Authorities found no explosives on any of the aircraft.
summary: Bomb threats were reported against two passenger planes bound for Warsaw, a Ryanair flight from London to Spain, two flights to Rome, and a flight from Israel to the Bulgarian capital Sofia. Authorities found no explosives on any of the aircraft.
author: DW World

title: UNICEF reports nearly 2,000 attacks on Ukrainian schools since 2022, 270 this year
content: UNICEF reported that Ukraine has suffered almost 2,000 attacks on education since the full‑scale Russian invasion began in 2022, with 270 incidents recorded this year alone. The announcement came a day after a strike on a school that was being used to distribute aid.
summary: Ukraine has sustained almost 2,000 attacks on education since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022. UNICEF said on Tuesday that about 270 of those attacks occurred this year, a day after a strike hit a school used to distribute aid.
author: UN News

title: Gender equality benefits business while companies pull back on initiatives
content: Gender equality and diversity are cited as beneficial to business. The piece notes that more women are reaching senior corporate positions, yet stresses that additional initiatives are required to maintain this momentum.
summary: Gender equality and diversity are good for business. More initiatives are needed to keep momentum going as increasing numbers of women reach top corporate spots.

title: Haiti gang leader seeks UN talks as El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to hunt for missing soldiers
content: A Haitian gang leader who is wanted by the United States has requested that the United Nations act as a mediator. At the same time, El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 troops into the country to locate four Salvadoran soldiers who disappeared following a gang ambush.
summary: Haiti gang leader seeks UN talks as El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to hunt for missing soldiers.

title: Yemeni 14‑year‑old Safa married to elderly man as war threatens family protection
content: Safa, a 14‑year‑old girl in Yemen, lost her mother earlier this year and has no brothers or sisters. As the crisis deepened, her father married her to an elderly man, saying he feared she would be left unprotected if he were killed in the hostilities. The case underscores the devastating consequences faced by women and girls in the war.
summary: Safa is 14, her mother died earlier this year, and she has no brothers or sisters. A few weeks ago, as the crisis took hold, her father married her to an elderly man, fearing that if he were killed in the hostilities she would have no protection.

title: Myanmar school airstrike kills three children, injures five, UNICEF says
content: UNICEF said an airstrike hit a school in Myanmar, killing three children and injuring five others. The organization reported the casualties but provided no further details about the incident.

title: UN warns drone strikes in Sudan disrupt electricity, water, fuel and aid
content: Intensifying drone attacks on civilian infrastructure across Sudan are disrupting electricity, water and fuel supplies, putting lives at risk and hampering the delivery of humanitarian aid, the UN’s top official in the country has warned.
summary: The UN’s top official in Sudan said intensifying drone attacks on civilian infrastructure are disrupting electricity, water and fuel supplies. The attacks are putting lives at risk and hampering the delivery of humanitarian aid.

title: Parliament building faces Notre Dame‑style fire risk as renovation costs surge
content:
A parliamentary committee has warned that the Palace of Westminster faces a “Notre Dame‑style” fire or a comparable catastrophic event unless Members of Parliament secure funding for its refurbishment. The committee noted that maintenance costs could soon rise to £2 million per week, a figure that includes 24‑hour patrols intended to prevent a fire.

Decisions on when and how to begin a full restoration have been repeatedly delayed, the committee said, because of disagreement over the approach and because costs are spiralling. The building is a Grade I‑listed structure and a UNESCO World Heritage site.
summary: A parliamentary committee warned that the Palace of Westminster could face a Notre Dame‑style fire if funding for refurbishments is not secured. The report estimates maintenance costs could soon reach £2 million a week, including 24‑hour patrols, as restoration plans have been repeatedly delayed amid cost disputes.
author: Guardian World

title: Canada joins coalition to bar Russian ice hockey teams from world junior championship
content: Growing number of countries are resisting Russia’s reintegration into international hockey after a sports court lifted a ban on competition Canada has joined a coalition of countries refusing to play ⁠ice ​hockey teams from Russia, with prime minister Mark Carney saying Russian skaters will not be able to compete in ⁠a world junior championship next month due to the war in Ukraine. “While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific ‌war in Ukraine, as long as that’s going on, there will be none of ​those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” Carney told reporters on Tuesday.
summary: Canada has joined a coalition of countries refusing to play ice hockey teams from Russia. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Russian skaters will be barred from the upcoming world junior championship because of the war in Ukraine.
author: Guardian World

title: UK apologises to Ukrainian child refugees over forced Russian study
content:
The UK has issued an apology to Ukrainian child refugees who were told to study Russian in English schools. The apology follows criticism that teachers suggested Russian in the absence of a Ukrainian GCSE. The Schools Minister announced the launch of a new Ukrainian GCSE and expressed regret over the situation.

Funding has been provided for the new Ukrainian GCSE, offering an alternative to Russian language instruction.

Ukrainian children, displaced after Vladimir Putin’s 2022 invasion, described the recommendation to study Russian as insulting.
summary: The UK has apologised to Ukrainian child refugees who were told to study Russian in English schools as it announced funding for a new Ukrainian GCSE. The children, who fled after Vladimir Putin’s invasion in 2022, said it was insulting that teachers suggested Russian study because there was no Ukrainian GCSE.
author: Guardian World

title: Victoria police: One Nation supporter attack not politically motivated, blunt weapon used
content:
Victoria police have stated that an alleged attack on a One Nation supporter was not politically motivated. They clarified that the attacker used a “blunt weapon” rather than a baseball bat, as initially reported.

Police confirmed on Tuesday that they had arrested a 37‑year‑old man from Hampton Park and a 14‑year‑old boy. The arrests relate to the alleged assault on a 60‑year‑old man outside his Torquay home on Sunday night.
summary: Police say the alleged attack on a 60-year-old One Nation supporter in Torquay is not believed to be politically motivated and involved a blunt weapon, not a baseball bat. Police arrested a 37-year-old Hampton Park man and a 14-year-old boy over the Sunday night assault.
author: Guardian World

title: Aukus submarine deal deemed worst Australian defence decision; inquiry urges suspension
content: Report led by Peter Garrett and former defence chief Adm Chris Barrie says agreement should be suspended and calls for royal commission Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast A public inquiry into the $368bn Aukus nuclear submarine agreement has called the plan “the worst, riskiest and most costly defence decision ever made by an Australian government”, urging its immediate termination. Former Labor MP and Midnight Oil frontman Peter Garrett and former chief of defence Adm Chris Barrie led the inquiry dominated by critics of the deal with the UK and US, recommending the suspension of plans for new bases and for a royal commission to be held into the agreement signed by the former Morrison government. summary: Aukus submarine deal deemed worst Australian defence decision; inquiry urges suspension.

title: David Jones likely to enter administration after failed talks with landlord Scentre Group
content:
David Jones, the 188‑year‑old upmarket department‑store chain, is expected to enter administration after 11th‑hour negotiations between its private‑equity owner and its primary landlord broke down. The talks with Westfield owner Scentre Group failed to produce an agreement, leaving the retailer’s future in doubt.

The situation follows years of steep losses, weak consumer spending and a string of underperforming stores that have caused the heritage retailer to default on its rent, prompting the current crisis.
summary: David Jones, the 188‑year‑old upmarket department store chain, is expected to go into administration after 11th‑hour talks between its private‑equity owner and primary landlord Scentre Group broke down. The retailer has faced years of steep losses, weak consumer spending and underperforming stores that left it defaulting on rent.
author: Guardian World

title: Kate McClymont questioned over ‘nail in the coffin’ comment and emoji text at Alan Jones trial
content: Award-winning investigative journalist says she ‘probably’ texted an alleged victim’s mother saying ‘I hope the shit does hit the fan for him’, court hears Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Investigative journalist Kate McClymont has told a Sydney court that an audio recording in which she said new information would be “an absolute nail in the coffin” did not refer to “killing” Alan Jones. In a phone call with the mother of the youngest alleged victim of Jones, which was played in court, the Sydney Morning Herald’s chief investigative reporter expressed excitement when the woman said her son had spoken to police in the same year as the alleged assault.
summary: Kate McClymont questioned over ‘nail in the coffin’ comment and emoji text at Alan Jones trial.

title: ANC faces anger over poor services as it heads for less than a third of local vote
content:
South Africans are heading to the polls on Wednesday for local elections amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure, prompting anger toward the African National Congress. The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 as the country’s first black president, is still expected to remain the largest party.

Polls show the ANC on course for a bruising result, with support projected at less than one‑third of the vote, down from 45.6 % in the 2021 municipal elections and 40.2 % in the 2024 national elections.
summary: The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections, with polls showing it likely to receive less than a third of the vote. title: NASA seeks industry ideas to extend Hubble Space Telescope's life
content: NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now. The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way. Hubble, which launched in April 1990 in partnership with the European Space Agency, was serviced five times by astronauts on space shuttle missions, the most recent being in 2009. The observatory's groundbreaking achievements include helping to show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating — a discovery that won the Nobel Prize — as well as a swath of finds about planets, galaxies, stars and other parts of the universe. Hubble also regularly teams up with other telescopes for science work, and its observations have led to the publication of at least 23,000 scientific papers, NASA figures suggest. And, despite its age, Hubble remains in high demand. "Astronomers request about seven times as much observing time as is available each year," the agency stated in September. Hubble is also widely appreciated by the public. People have long enjoyed and celebrated its iconic images, such as the Eagle Nebula's "Pillars of Creation," a gorgeous shot that has been revisited several times over the decades. As such, this is not the first time in recent years that discussions have opened about keeping the famed observatory running for a while longer. In 2022, for example, billionaire tech entrepreneur Jared Isaacman proposed using SpaceX hardware to mount a Hubble-servicing mission. (Isaacman also purchased and commanded two crewed SpaceX missions to Earth orbit, which flew in September 2021 and September 2024.) NASA declined, however, citing possible risks to the healthy observatory. But things have changed, apparently. Isaacman, who in December 2025 became NASA administrator, said in an Oct. 30 agency statement that Hubble's science return means the agency should "be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible" — especially if doing so would be a cost savings compared with launching another mission. In an Oct. 30 post on X, Isaacman added that it's "still worth exploring the options" and noted that NASA had previously considered "a far lower-cost solution" to keep the observatory flying. "That was then. Still worth the effort — Hubble deserves it," he added. The new RFI also allows for alternative scenarios, however, which could include a "safe, controlled reentry into Earth's atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble's mission." Hubble will naturally enter the atmosphere in 2033 or 2034 due to orbital drag, so any attempt to service it would have to be in 2032, the agency stated. Earlier this year, NASA worked with Katalyst Space Technologies on a $30 million mission that aimed to boost the orbit of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which is also falling back to Earth due to orbital drag. That long-shot rescue mission — which was developed quickly to race against accelerated solar activity, which ballooned Earth's atmosphere and increased drag — launched successfully this summer. But control issues prevented Katalyst's LINK spacecraft from meeting up with Swift. Swift is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere tomorrow (Nov. 4) after 22 years of operations — far past its two-year design lifetime.
summary: NASA issued a request for information on in-space servicing options to boost the Hubble Space Telescope's orbit before it reenters the atmosphere in 2033 or 2034. Administrator Jared Isaacman stated that the agency should explore every reasonable opportunity to keep the observatory operating to maximize its science return.

title: The Gilded Age returns for fourth season despite negative reviews
content: Julian Fellowes’ high-society period drama has, somehow, picked up Emmys and reached its fourth series. Poor Meryl Streep must feel so awkward watching her daughter Louisa Jacobson in such a uniformly awful show A doctor with a fully qualified moustache races up a carriageway towards an immaculate stately home. “I fear we should have sent for you sooner!” says the lady who greets him on the doorstep as the screams of a woman in drug-free labour rattle the windows in their frames. Oh, ya think? Is not Dr Moustache’s reply. When this many cliches assemble so quickly, it can only mean one thing: Brownstone Abbey – AKA Julian Fellowes’ Revenge, AKA What Did We Do to Deserve This?, AKA The Gilded Age if you insist on its official title – is back for a fourth and, no one has said let alone promised, final season.

title: Randy Boyagoda's 'Lords of Serendipity' satirizes higher‑education corruption
content: This propulsive, globe-trotting tale brilliantly skewers the corruption and corporatisation of higher education It’s no secret that academia is on the blink; Canadian author Randy Boyagoda’s new novel, which is equal parts satire, dystopia and exposé, tells the story of all that’s wrong, glitchy and broken. Set across Sri Lanka, the United States and Italy, it centres on a cast of students, parents and professors, and their dealings with a common antagonist: the university. The first character we meet is Sri Lankan teen Devi, who is set on obtaining offers from “Ochpys” – her acronym for Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Princeton, Yale and Stanford. To help her realise her dream, Devi’s family of modest means – her mother, father, maternal grandmother and two brothers – hire themselves out as mourners at the funerals of the wealthy. Most of this money goes towards paying Johannes, her tutor on WhatsApp who, unbeknown to Devi, is a hard-up Indian student at Arcadia Tech, an undistinguished university in the US. Meanwhile, Jack, a statistician at the same institution, has taken on an additional teaching load to meet the fees of the elite college his daughter Katrina attends in New England. Soon he catches on to a grade-fixing scheme aimed at flailing international students, run by his teaching assistant Allard Hamburger. Jack is left in disbelief when, to buy his silence, the university puts him on paid administrative leave instead of launching an inquiry into a scandal that has left one student dead by suicide.
summary: The novel is a globe‑trotting satire that skewers the corruption and corporatisation of higher education. It follows Sri Lankan teen Devi, her family's funeral‑mourners scheme, a hard‑up Indian tutor, and a statistician who uncovers a grade‑fixing scandal that the university brushes aside with paid administrative leave.

title: West Ham sack Nuno Espírito Santo after losing three of 13 Championship matches
content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! While Football Daily hasn’t actually seen much of West Ham this season, we’ve noted enough of their results to presume they were doing OK in their attempt to bounce back to the Premier League after relegation. Less than a third of the way through the Championship season under Nuno Espírito Santo, they’d already spanked six without reply past both Wrexham and Lincoln, while scoring three or more in wins over Wolves, Derby and Bolton. However, it turns out that of the 13 matches they’ve played in a league that is famously difficult to get out of (unless you were Sheffield Wednesday last season ), they have actually lost three times and currently sit in eighth place, a whopping six points off leaders Middlesbrough. Given the context of such an unbridgeable chasm, it is small wonder West Ham fans woke up to news that Nuno had been unceremoniously bounced out of the London Stadium with a P45 in hand. While my heart aches for Jesús de Miguel, who has died after a collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono, I shudder to think the trauma that shall haunt Owono for the rest of his life. I do hope and pray the wider community understands and extends their support in his recuperation” – Krishna Moorthy. As an upgrade to Steve Plever’s suggestion of paper thin shirts [ Monday’s letters ]: how about Velcro shirts? If the bit comes off, it is a shirt pull and the offender has the honour of putting it back in place before being awarded a yellow card” – Mike Harold. To dive or not to dive seems to be biggest dilemma in the Premier League right now. It’s not. The problem with today’s highly paid professionals is that they simply have no panache at all when they go down. I recall watching Francis Lee pick up the ball on the halfway line at a mud soaked Maine Road in the late 1960s, he put his head down and headed for goal, he was determined, he was single minded. He was 30 yards from goal, he was in full flow. He was tackled from behind and then he really took off, he grew wings, he soared. I swear he landed in the penalty area over 10 yards away. He dragged himself to his feet and without a semblance of a smile smashed the well-deserved penalty, with a very heavy leather ball straight at the centre of the goal at over 70 mph. The goalkeeper, obviously no fool, simply dived out of the way. The press christened him “Lee Won Pen” He was my hero. That man had panache, he had style” – Myles Flynn. content:

The 2-1 defeat in August marked a historic but disappointing outcome for the squad, which holds the record for the most decorated national side in Africa across both men’s and women’s football, with ten Wafcon titles to its name.

title: Glenn Maxwell's six greatest innings for Australia
content:
Glenn Maxwell has retired from international cricket, ending a career marked by both spectacular performances and a lingering perception of unfulfilled potential. The 38-year-old was not selected for Australia’s T20 squad to face England this month, which prevented him from making a final appearance for the national team before concluding his international tenure.

Maxwell’s legacy includes several high-impact innings, such as a rare Test century, game-changing centuries, and a notable performance in Mumbai. As a three-time World Cup winner, he is also credited with what is described as arguably the greatest ODI knock of all time. These standout moments define his reputation as a destructive batsman who utilized unconventional shots to alter the course of matches.
summary: Glenn Maxwell has retired from international cricket after being overlooked for Australia's T20 squad to face England. The 38-year-old three-time World Cup winner is remembered for destructive knocks, including a rare Test century and a historic ODI performance in Mumbai.

Although Kane did not score, he expressed hope that the match would help replace bad memories with good ones as he prepares for a potential return to the venue on 5 June for another chance at winning the competition.

While Atlético Madrid managed to resist for a period, their defense ultimately held out for only 54 minutes. Lennart Karl broke the deadlock with the opening goal, followed by a second goal from Konrad Laimer. Bayern Munich recorded nineteen shots on target, demonstrating a team with few weaknesses that proved to be just too good for their opponents.

title: Foot-stiffening socks reduce running energy use by 2%
content:
Researchers at the University of Texas at Austin have developed foot-stiffening socks that appear to reduce the energy required for walking and running. Owen Beck and Hui Tang, both affiliated with the university, created the socks by tightly knitting three millimetre-wide bands into a 30-millimetre region around the ball of the foot. This design applies 24 times more pressure to the feet than regular control socks, effectively increasing foot stiffness. The researchers note that human feet have naturally become stiffer than those of other apes over millions of years to support bipedalism, and their work explores whether further stiffness in footwear can enhance movement efficiency.

To evaluate the socks, Beck and Tang recruited 12 healthy adults of both sexes to walk on a treadmill while wearing the stiffened socks, control socks, or no socks. The team measured the participants’ VO2 max, the maximum amount of oxygen the body can absorb during high-intense exercise, to determine metabolic expenditure. The results showed that the foot-stiffening socks reduced metabolic expenditure by 2 per cent in 10 of the 12 participants compared to the control socks. The researchers state that this reduction is equivalent to the energy savings an average person would experience from losing two kilograms.

Beck explains that the socks work by allowing the ankle and its muscles to push off at a slower velocity, which requires less muscle activation and metabolic energy. Unlike stiffened shoes, which can restrict necessary foot movements at the end of a step, these socks permit the toes to flex and the arch to recoil more freely. Beck estimates that wrapping the foot in these new socks could improve marathon performance by one to two minutes, with hopes that elite runners might use them at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. He also suggests that the reduced whole-body metabolic rate could lead to better walking endurance and less sweating on hot days.

While the findings are promising, independent experts have offered cautious perspectives. Thomas Püschel at the University of Oxford notes that the idea of a stiff foot reducing metabolic cost has long existed, but previous attempts using stiff midsoles or inserts in shoes failed because they prevented necessary foot movement. Püschel warns that other explanations for the results cannot be ruled out, such as volunteers altering their gait because they knew they were wearing the socks. He describes the study as a promising first demonstration rather than definitive evidence that the socks will change daily life.

The research team has a sponsored research agreement with shoe company New Balance to commercialise the socks. Beck suggests that in theory, anyone whose feet have lost some of their shape, such as through old age, could benefit from the technology. The study was published in the Royal Society Proceedings B.
summary: Foot-stiffening socks reduce running energy use by 2%.

title: Finic launches Kairos, open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
content:
Show HN: Kairos – Open‑source risk and fraud decisioning platform

Ayan from Finic announced the launch of Kairos, an open‑source alternative to commercial real‑time fraud decisioning platforms such as Sift and Sardine. Kairos is designed to address two key challenges that traditional fraud tools face.

First, many businesses lack the large, high‑quality labeled data sets required by machine‑learning models like XGBoost. Kairos mitigates this by incorporating “System One” decision models alongside conventional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This approach lets users embed plain‑language questions—e.g., “Is this a throwaway email”—into the decision workflow, reducing dependence on extensive labeled data and better capturing unstructured fraud signals that XGBoost struggles with.

Second, fraudsters continually evolve tactics, rendering static detection rules and models obsolete within weeks. To keep pace, Kairos introduces an MCP server that allows an agent—such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex—to define a decision workflow, train models on an organization’s own data, and select the variant that performs best. This reduces the need for a large data‑science team to constantly retrain models and update rules.

Kairos can be self‑hosted with Docker or accessed via the hosted service at https://kairos.finic.ai. The announcement received 37 points and four comments on Hacker News.
summary: Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms.
author: Hacker News

title: Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 hit lowest price of $169 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Google Store
content:
The Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 are currently available for $169, matching their lowest price to date. This discount is active at Amazon, Best Buy, and the Google Store, reducing the cost from the standard $229 price tag. According to Google’s website, the offer will remain in place until 11:59 PM PT on November 8th, with other retailers expected to match the deal. Shoppers should note that certain color options are already sold out, suggesting it may be necessary to check multiple retailers to find a preferred variant.

The earbuds are designed for Android users and offer enhanced features, such as tighter Gemini integration, when paired with Pixel phones. The hardware features an improved design that reduces weight and size while increasing comfort and fit. Audio performance includes more powerful noise cancellation and an upgraded transparency mode, although these features do not fully match industry leaders like the latest Bose Ultra Earbuds. The default sound tuning prioritizes clarity and crisp detail over boosted bass, and users can customize the audio experience using various presets and a five-band equalizer.

Additional deals are also available for tech consumers. Nintendo Switch owners can purchase Borderlands: Game of the Year Edition for $5.99, a significant drop from its usual $29.99 price, until 11:59 PM PT on November 6th. This edition includes visual upgrades and all four DLC packs. In the coffee maker market, the refurbished Fellow Aiden is priced at $299.95, offering a $100 discount. This unit brews pour-over-quality coffee with scheduling capabilities and comes with a one-year warranty. Finally, Prime Members can obtain a 25-watt ESR Cyclone Magnetic Charging Pad for $36.99, a 26 percent discount that includes a built-in fan and an integrated stand.
summary: The Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 are discounted to $169 at Amazon, Best Buy, and the Google Store, matching their lowest price to date. Google states the deal will last until 11:59PM PT on November 8th, though some colors are already sold out.
author: The Verge

title: Those Jeff Bezos hair transplant photos are very fake
content:
Photos of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and actor Jason Statham featuring significantly more hair have circulated on social media platforms X, Threads, and Bluesky. The images, which depict the two men with substantial hair growth—appearing as a fresh transplant in Bezos’ case—are confirmed to be photo editing fakery, whether created using AI or other methods. The Verge notes that while the edits are jarring, the prevalence of these posts has been enough for several members of their team to encounter them in their feeds.

The viral images contrast sharply with the reality that both Bezos and Statham remain famously bald, a condition that has not changed in recent days. Although the exact scale of the posts' virality is unclear, they have become prevalent enough to draw attention from media outlets investigating the authenticity of the circulating content.
summary: These edits of Jason Statham (left) and Jeff Bezos are a bit jarring, but that’s sort of the point. | Image: The Verge Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and actor Jason Statham have a distinctive feature in common: They're both famously bald, and that definitely hasn't changed in the last few days.
author: The Verge

title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 gain Live Rewind and Siri Recap in watchOS 27.3 beta
content:
The Verge has shared initial impressions of the Audio Intelligence features available in the watchOS 27.3 developer beta for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. The publication notes that it is currently impossible to provide a complete assessment of these capabilities, as they are intended for day-to-day use. The Verge plans to test the features over the coming weeks to offer a more comprehensive review.

Newly available in the beta are Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind allows users to view a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio, while Siri Recap provides high-level summaries of conversations. The article mentions that two other Audio Intelligence features have been available for some time, though the text cuts off before specifying which ones. The Verge also acknowledges that Siri can still make mistakes in its transcripts.
summary: The watchOS 27.3 developer beta introduces Live Rewind, which displays a transcript of the last 15 seconds, and Siri Recap, which provides high-level conversation summaries. These Audio Intelligence features are available on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, though Siri may still make mistakes in transcripts.
author: The Verge

title: Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to pull off the $6.3 billion heist
content:
Binance attributes the largest cryptocurrency theft to date, valued at $6.3 billion, to a multi-month campaign that combined established hacking techniques with an internal AI tool. According to the company’s postmortem, the operation began in June when a developer downloaded a tampered installer distributed via a malicious Google ad. This action exposed details regarding the engineers and their operational methods.

In September, the attackers targeted another engineer by impersonating a potential employer. The individual conducted multiple interview calls and shared social media pages to establish trust, ultimately tricking the employee into downloading a fake interview assignment.
summary: Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to pull off the $6.3 billion heist.
author: The Verge

title: Valve Extends Steam Game Review Times to 12 Business Days
content:
Valve has acknowledged a significant increase in Steam game submissions, resulting in review times extending to up to 12 business days compared to the typical 3-5 days. The company stated it is currently running behind on store and page reviews, a delay that has frustrated indie developers and caused some games to miss their planned launch dates.

To address the backlog, Valve identified re-reviews of games for basic functional issues as a major cause of the delays. The company is implementing changes to the release checklist for developers, aiming to reduce the need for re-reviews and streamline the approval process.
summary: Valve is extending Steam game review times to up to 12 business days due to a significant increase in submissions. The company is updating the release checklist to reduce re‑reviews for basic functional issues.
author: The Verge

title: Sonos launches Presets and opens US waitlist for 27voice AI beta
content:
Sonos has released a major app update introducing new Presets and early access to its AI voice assistant. The Presets feature allows users to create specific commands that play music at a designated volume in a particular room. These custom presets appear directly on the app’s homescreen, enabling quick playback initiation.

In the United States, users can sign up for the waitlist for the Sonos 27voice assistant on November 6th. Access to the beta version of the assistant is scheduled to begin on November 12th. Sonos previously teased that the 27voice assistant will allow users to start music, move playback to different rooms, group and ungroup speakers, and set timers. The company also noted that the assistant is capable of completing more complex tasks, though the specific details of these capabilities were cut off in the provided text.
summary: Sonos is rolling out an app update that allows users to create music presets for specific rooms and volumes on the homescreen. US users can sign up for the 27voice AI assistant waitlist on November 6th, with access beginning on November 12th.
author: The Verge

title: Canva to lay off 22% of staff, 1,271 employees, as CEO announces changes
content:
Canva co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins announced that the company will implement significant changes affecting 1,271 employees, representing 22 percent of its staff. Perkins stated that these adjustments include role modifications or requests for staff to relocate to centralized hubs. She acknowledged that the restructuring will also result in the departure of teammates who contributed to the company’s development.

In a note to staff, Perkins explained that after exploring various alternatives, she concluded that minor adjustments would be insufficient. She said the company needs to "refound Canva" and return to its roots of being small to prepare for the next decade.
summary: Canva's co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins announced that 1,271 people, or 22 percent of the company's staff, will be affected by changes that include role adjustments, relocations, and layoffs. The announcement comes after the company explored alternatives but decided that small changes would not be enough to prepare Canva for the next decade.
author: The Verge

title: Pimco CEO Says He Does Not Know When AI Bubble Will Pop
content:
Emmanuel Roman, chief executive officer of Pacific Investment Management Co. (Pimco), spoke at the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit in Hong Kong, China, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. During the event, he noted that people repeatedly ask him when the AI bubble will burst. Roman replied that if he knew the answer, he would place a significant market bet, leverage up, and then retire on a beach or possibly run a cat sanctuary.

Roman also mentioned a Bloomberg story published that morning titled “Wall Street CEOs, Big Money Managers Divided Over AI Risks.” The piece is a roundup of remarks made at the 2026 summit, and it captured Roman’s attention. He used the article to illustrate the broader conversation among financial leaders about the risks and opportunities of artificial intelligence.
summary: Pimco CEO Emmanuel Roman stated that he does not know when the AI bubble will burst, noting he would make a levered bet if he knew. He referenced a Bloomberg article about Wall Street CEOs being divided over AI risks at a Hong Kong summit.
author: The Verge

title: New York reports first measles death in 30 years
content:
A child in New York died of measles, according to state health officials who announced the death late Monday. This incident marks the first reported measles-associated death in New York in over 30 years. It is the seventh measles-linked death reported in the United States this year, with the other six occurring in Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania is currently experiencing a significant measles outbreak that has affected more than 1,430 people this year, representing the state’s first measles-related death in 35 years.

The article attributes the rise in vaccine-preventable outbreaks and deaths to declining vaccination rates fueled by health misinformation and anti-vaccine sentiments. It identifies Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the current US health secretary, as a prominent anti-vaccine activist who spent decades attacking vaccines and spreading misinformation before taking office. Since assuming his role, Kennedy has been reported to have dismantled and obstructed federal vaccine recommendations, launched studies into alleged vaccine harms, and promoted misinformation regarding vaccine injuries and preventable illnesses.
summary: A child in New York died of measles, marking the first reported measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years. This incident brings the total number of measles-linked deaths reported in the US this year to seven.
author: Ars Technica

title: Google Allows Schools to Opt Out of AI Tools but Must Drop Search
content:
Google has announced that schools using its education products will be opted out of AI tools by default, giving administrators the choice to manually enable these features in the coming months. The company stated that this decision follows consultations with educators, researchers, and lawmakers. While Google is working to expand beyond Chromebooks, the widespread use of these devices has established a significant presence for its education products in schools.

However, the new policy creates a difficult trade-off for educators. Google has categorized Google Search alongside its AI products, including Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Gemini in Classroom. Under the new rules, schools cannot selectively block only the AI tools; opting out of AI features also means giving up access to Google Search. Consequently, administrators must choose to allow all the specified tools or none of them, leaving schools with a limited set of options for managing digital resources in the classroom.
summary: Google will let schools opt out of its AI tools by default, but doing so requires them to forgo Google Search. Administrators must manually enable all AI tools—Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search—if they wish to use them in K‑12 classrooms.
author: Ars Technica

title: Buttons are back and storage is king when it comes to car interiors
content: As with interior design for houses, interior design for vehicles is also subject to fashion trends. And like any fashion trend, even the best ideas can become stale and played out with overuse. Some ideas weren’t the best, either, like demonstrably worse human-machine interfaces that add to driver distraction; yet, they still proliferated throughout the industry and across the cars offered for sale. But the good news is that the pushback seems to be working. “When the trend of the Piano Black and the switchless interior was happening, it was during a time when designers and companies and engineers and everybody were thinking that, 'Hey, we can just get rid of all these switches on the interior. We can put it all in the software. It'll save money. It'll save us tooling up all these extra parts for unique cars and all this stuff and make the interior more like a software experience.' And it was done with those intentions,” said Hiren Patel, senior design manager at Nissan. That resulted in cars with minimalist interiors that looked good in the dealership. But people drive their cars on roads; they don’t just sit inside them, parked inside a dealership. “So lots of people were complaining about it and saying, 'Hey, it takes my eyes off the road to change the temperature or to adjust my seat or do whatever.' It's not as easy as doing something on your phone where it's just right at your fingertips and intuitive,” Patel said. Read full article Comments
summary: Interior designers once removed switches to create minimalist, software‑centric car interiors, but drivers complained the changes distracted them from the road. Senior design manager Hiren Patel of Nissan says the trend is reversing, with buttons returning to improve usability.
author: Ars Technica

title: NYT sues Brave for bypassing paywalls and selling content to AI firms
content: The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies. "Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere," the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that "Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission," while "publishers have received nothing." The lawsuit said, "AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index," and use content from the Brave index "to train their own AI models" and "to respond to specific user queries." The NYT lawsuit points to Brave's website, which says the Brave Search API is "used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You. Com." Read full article Comments
summary: NYT sues Brave for bypassing paywalls and selling content to AI firms.
author: Ars Technica

title: Ukraine drone strikes prompt Russian tech firms to move data centers underground
content:
Russian technology firms are rapidly working to relocate and secure their data centers underground after Ukrainian drone attacks damaged facilities that house AI supercomputers and disrupted cloud services for millions of Russian users. In response, the Kremlin has mandated that data center owners reserve computing capacity for emergency state needs and has authorized the possible use of foreign data centers.

These measures come amid a broader context of Russian military activity, which has bombarded Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles almost continuously in recent months and has specifically targeted Ukrainian data centers since late September. Ukraine, in turn, has struck back with drone attacks on Russian military and infrastructure targets, degrading or knocking out data centers operated by Yandex, Sberbank, VKontakte, and the Ministry of Finance.

State‑owned telecommunications company Rostelcom has reportedly discussed moving some Russian data centers underground with nickel and palladium mining company Norilsk, as reported by Vedomosti. Additionally, Data Center Dynamics cited a proposal by a Russian regional governor to construct data centers inside open‑pit coal mines, with green public parks planted above as camouflage.
summary: Ukraine drone strikes prompt Russian tech firms to move data centers underground.
author: Ars Technica

title: California Accepts $1.42B Broadband Grant, Rejects Trump Demand to Drop Net Neutrality
content:
California has agreed to accept $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but it has rejected the federal demand that the state stop enforcing its net neutrality law and other telecom regulations. The state’s refusal could lead to multiple legal battles among California, the federal government and internet providers that rely on government funds.

California has told the federal government it will take the money, but it is reserving the right to challenge the condition that it must abandon its net‑neutrality and other regulatory rules. Depending on how the dispute unfolds, the state could delay or cancel its plans to distribute the broadband grants.

Last year the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided that states receiving money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net‑neutrality rule on ISPs. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction.

California is slated to spend the $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations, and it may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non‑deployment projects.
summary: California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration. The state refuses to comply with the administration's demand to stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations, potentially leading to legal battles.
author: Ars Technica

title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics before $6.3B Binance heist
content: Cybersecurity researchers had warned for years about the persistent and patient threat posed by North Korea’s long‑running hacking operations. Despite these cautions, the world’s largest crypto exchange was still caught off‑guard when a record $6.3 billion heist occurred.
summary: Cybersecurity experts have long warned of the persistent and patient threat from North Korea's long‑running hacks. The world's largest crypto exchange was still caught off‑guard by a record $6.3B Binance heist.
author: TechCrunch

title: Data centers turn to discarded jet engines amid grid access delays
content: Data center builders are turning to discarded jet engines because of a years‑long wait for access to the grid and new turbines. This unconventional choice is less efficient and less environmentally friendly.
summary: Data center builders are using discarded jet engines because of a long wait for grid access and new turbines. This solution is less efficient and less environmentally friendly.
author: TechCrunch

title: Google says Search requires AI; schools can block AI but lose Search access
content:
Google announced that users cannot use Google Search without artificial intelligence. In a school‑focused announcement on Tuesday, the company introduced a slate of new AI products for classrooms and schools and outlined additional options for teachers and schools to limit or restrict those AI tools.

The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom. However, if a school or teacher blocks the use of Google’s AI features, students will be unable to use Google Search.
summary: Google announced new AI products for classrooms and said students cannot use Google Search if AI features are blocked. The company emphasized that schools should control AI use in the classroom.
author: Guardian Technology

title: US tech stocks recover after AI spending selloff spooks investors
content:
US technology shares rebounded on Tuesday afternoon after a sharp selloff that had investors concerned about corporate spending on artificial‑intelligence projects. The rally helped lift the sector’s overall performance for the day.

The day’s movements appeared largely unrelated to the midterm election results. Wall Street did not show a significant reaction to the votes cast in the election.

Analysts note that Democrats are expected to secure at least a majority in the House and could gain seats in the Senate. Such a shift could pave the way for increased regulation of AI, according to market observers.
summary: US tech stocks recovered on Tuesday afternoon after a selloff that worried investors about AI spending. The midterm elections had little effect on Wall Street, but predictions of a Democratic majority could lead to increased AI regulation.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Korkmaz Enes Ergun Detained on Bribe and Crime Organization Charges
content:
Turkey's justice minister said a criminal network was behind a billion‑dollar fund scandal, highlighting the scale of the alleged wrongdoing.  

In the investigation, Korkmaz Enes Ergun was detained on 31 October and remanded on charges of accepting bribes and membership of an organization formed to commit crimes.
summary: Korkmaz Enes Ergun was detained on 31 October. He was remanded on charges of accepting bribes and membership of an organization formed to commit crimes.
author: Euronews

title: Russia double‑tap strike on Ukrainian aid school kills at least 31
content: A Russian “double tap” strike on a Ukrainian school being used as an aid distribution has killed at least 31 people, according to local authorities, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky dubbing it a “vile terrorist attack”.
summary: Russia double‑tap strike on Ukrainian aid school kills at least 31.
author: France 24

title: Brazil watches US midterm elections as ties with Trump grow tense
content: Brazil is closely monitoring the United States midterm elections, according to a report by FRANCE 24. The outlet notes that relations between Brasilia and Washington have become increasingly tense since Donald Trump returned to the White House. On the economic side, aggressive trade policies have imposed some of the steepest tariffs worldwide on Brazilian imports, heightening friction with the Trump administration. FRANCE 24’s correspondent in Rio de Janeiro, Jan Onoszko, provides further details.
summary: Brazil is closely monitoring the United States midterm elections. Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, relations between Brasilia and Washington have become increasingly tense, with aggressive trade policies imposing steep tariffs on Brazilian imports and heightening friction with the Trump administration.
author: France 24

title: State officials prepare for possible Trump interference in Tuesday midterms
content: State officials who oversee U.S. elections said they are preparing for possible intervention by President Donald Trump’s administration in the Tuesday midterm elections. They warned that federal authorities loyal to the president could disrupt voting, contest ballot counts, or attempt to block certification of results they consider unfavorable.
summary: State officials who run US elections braced for possible intervention by President Donald Trump's administration in Tuesday's midterms. They fear federal authorities loyal to the president could disrupt voting, challenge ballot counts or try to block certification of unfavorable results.
author: France 24

title: Trump’s “Golden Age” promise examined after 2025 domestic policy actions
content: Donald Trump promised Americans a “Golden Age” when he returned to the White House in January 2025. Since then, his administration has slashed government spending through DOGE, ramped up mass deportations, expanded ICE operations and pursued an aggressive crackdown on DEI programmes and transgender rights. But how much has he actually achieved, and at what cost? Vedika Bahl examines Trump's domestic agenda since returning to office.
summary: Donald Trump promised Americans a “Golden Age” when he returned to the White House in January 2025. Since then his administration has slashed government spending through DOGE, increased mass deportations and ICE operations, and aggressively cracked down on DEI programmes and transgender rights, a domestic agenda reviewed by Vedika Bahl.
author: France 24

title: South Africa braces for job losses as AGOA duty‑free access ends
content:
Rwanda and South Africa will lose their duty‑free access to the U.S. market after being excluded from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade program, a development that analysts say could lead to job losses in South Africa.  

At the same time, South Africans are heading to the polls while coping with water shortages and frustration over local services.  

In the Democratic Republic of Congo’s mining capital, Kolwezi, residents are confronting one of the country’s largest Chinese‑owned mines, accusing the operation of poisoning the environment.
summary: In tonight's edition, Rwanda and South Africa will lose their duty-free access to the U. S.
author: France 24

title: Trump tariffs cause surge in small business bankruptcies
content: As US voters cast ballots in the midterm elections, the economy remained their top concern, even as headline macroeconomic data appeared robust. Middle‑class Americans expressed growing frustration with the rising cost of living, and correspondents reported that Donald Trump’s tariffs have hit small businesses hard, contributing to a notable increase in bankruptcies.
summary: As US voters cast ballots in the midterm elections, the economy remained their top concern. Donald Trump's tariffs have hit small businesses hard, leading to a significant rise in bankruptcies, according to business owners met by correspondents.
author: France 24

title: Historian Timothy Snyder says Trump runs US foreign policy like an organized criminal
content: As Americans head to the polls for the midterm elections, François Picard welcomes historian Timothy Snyder, professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs, for a conversation about the future of American democracy, the growing political influence of technology billionaires and the dangers of a new Gilded Age. Who really holds power in Donald Trump's America: the president or the billionaires surrounding him?
summary: Historian Timothy Snyder says Trump runs US foreign policy like an organized criminal.
author: France 24

title: AP survey finds 60% disapprove of Trump, economy and democracy top voter concerns
content: An AP survey released Tuesday finds roughly six‑in‑ten voters deeply disapprove of President Donald Trump’s presidency. About four‑in‑ten say the economy is the most important issue, three‑in‑ten prioritize the state of U.S. democracy, and concerns about the cost of living also rank among voters’ top issues, outpacing crime and immigration.
summary: AP survey finds 60% disapprove of Trump, economy and democracy top voter concerns.
author: France 24

title: Eight ways the US midterm election may shape Donald Trump's Iran policy
content: DW interviewed analysts who outlined eight factors by which the upcoming U.S. midterm elections could influence Donald Trump’s policy toward Iran. The analysts said the elections might create an opportunity for diplomatic engagement, but they could also trigger a new military escalation, depending on how those eight variables shift the balance between war and peace.
summary: The US midterm election could open a window for diplomacy with Iran or unleash a new military escalation. DW interviewed analysts who identified eight factors that could tip the balance toward war or peace.
author: DW World

title: Reform UK councillor George Madgwick charged with 12 rapes and child image offence
content:
George Madgwick, 37, the leader of the Reform group on Hampshire County Council and a Portsmouth councillor, has been charged with 12 counts of rape and one count of distributing indecent images of a child. The offences are alleged to involve four teenagers and span the period from 2008 to 2021.

Madgwick, who has been identified as a prominent voice in recent Portsmouth protests concerning the arrival of asylum seekers on small boats, now faces these serious criminal charges.
summary: Reform UK councillor George Madgwick charged with 12 rapes and child image offence.
author: Guardian World

title: King Charles urges addressing past wrongs at Commonwealth summit amid slavery apology calls
content:
King Charles addressed leaders at the opening of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday. Speaking in Antigua, he said he wanted to “address past wrongs” but did not give explicit support for reparations. He noted that his deepening understanding of the horrors of slavery has made him more determined to confront the wrongs of the past.

Caribbean leaders and campaigners have intensified demands for an apology and reparations from Britain. In his remarks, Charles acknowledged that “we cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” but added that “we can, however, learn from the past.”
summary: King Charles told leaders at the opening of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda that he wants to address past wrongs related to slavery. He did not give explicit support for reparations as Caribbean leaders and campaigners intensified demands for a British apology and reparations.
author: Guardian World

title: Family archive reveals private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, praised by Yeats
content:
A newly uncovered family archive provides a rare look at Rabindranath Tagore’s artistic process and personal relationships during his final years. The material, described as previously unseen, sheds light on the private creative world of the Indian Nobel laureate.

Tagore, born in 1861, is noted as the first non‑European to receive the Nobel Prize in literature and is recognized for his work as a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator. His contributions include the national anthems of India and Bangladesh, reflecting his lasting influence on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art.
summary: A previously unseen family archive provides insight into Rabindranath Tagore’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final years. Tagore, the first non‑European Nobel laureate in literature, was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator, whose legacies include the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
author: Guardian World

title: Trump says US will end $4bn Israel military aid by year‑end
content: US president makes surprise election day announcement, saying country does not ‘need’ $4bn annual payment Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year in a surprise election day announcement that appeared to be targeted at voters sceptical of US support for Israel and the war in Gaza. In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began on Tuesday morning, the US president said the US would cut nearly $4bn (£2.96bn) in military aid to Israel because “they don’t need it”.
summary: Trump says US will end $4bn Israel military aid by year‑end.
author: Guardian World

title: Spanish transport minister Óscar Puente resigns after train crash that killed 69
content: Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, submitted his resignation on Tuesday following a train crash that killed 69 people the previous week, an incident described as one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century. In the same statement, Puente announced that he will withdraw from the country’s upcoming general election. He had earlier pledged to work “tirelessly” to restore confidence in Spain’s high‑speed rail network, which is the world’s second‑largest.
summary: Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente handed in his resignation on Tuesday after a train crash that killed 69 people the previous week. He also announced that he is withdrawing from the country’s upcoming general election.
author: Guardian World

title: Two Australians confirmed dead in Spain high‑speed train crash
content:
Spanish authorities have confirmed the identities of three additional victims in the high‑speed train collision that killed 69 people last week. The new victims include two Australians and a Japanese citizen, none of whom have been named.

The identification work is being carried out by a legal body composed of police and forensic experts. The group announced the confirmation in a statement issued late on Monday. No further details about the victims have been released.
summary: Two Australians are among the 69 people killed in a high‑speed train collision in Spain, according to authorities. A police‑forensic identification body said the latest confirmed victims are two Australians and a Japanese citizen, whose names have not been released.
author: Guardian World

title: Choice Shonky Awards 2026 name $1,650 tickets, $75m airline credits, 25‑hour laundry cycle as worst
content:
Consumer advocacy group Choice has announced the winners of its 2026 Shonky Awards, naming Australia’s worst products and services for the year. Among the dishonour roll are concert tickets that have risen to $1,650, an airline that has retained $75 million in unused flight credits, and a washer‑dryer model with a 25‑hour cycle.

The awards, now in their 21st year, highlight the most criticised offerings as judged by Choice, aiming to draw attention to poor value and performance for Australian consumers.
summary: Consumer advocacy group Choice announced its 2026 Shonky Awards, naming Australia’s worst products and services. The list includes concert tickets that surged to $1,650, an airline pocketing $75 million of unused flight credits, and a washer/dryer cycle that takes 25 hours.
author: Guardian World

title: Mother dead, daughter missing after suspected grizzly bear attack in British Columbia
content:
A mother was found dead and her 19‑year‑old daughter remains missing after a suspected grizzly bear attack in a community in western Canada. The incident occurred in the same province where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren last November.

The British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said in a social‑media post that it began a search for the two people over the weekend. An officer discovered the mother’s body during the Sunday search, and the search for the daughter continues.
summary: A mother was found dead and her 19‑year‑old daughter remains missing after a suspected grizzly bear attack in a community in British Columbia. The British Columbia conservation officer service launched a search over the weekend and continues to look for the daughter.
author: Guardian World

title: Do we know how many Starship launches SpaceX will need to get NASA astronauts to the moon? No. Will its refuelling plan be simple? Also no.
content:
NASA’s Artemis IV mission, the program’s first crewed lunar landing, faces significant logistical complexities, particularly regarding the refueling requirements for SpaceX’s Starship if it serves as the lunar lander. Estimates for the number of refueling flights have varied widely; a 2021 Government Accountability Office audit suggested up to 16 launches might be necessary. More recently, a member of the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel estimated the number could be as high as 22, a figure SpaceX CEO Elon Musk refuted on social media, stating the requirement would likely be closer to six or eight.

The specific mechanics of the refueling process remain a subject of scrutiny. According to a graphic released by NASA during a recent Artemis update, the operation involves a staggered orbital staging strategy. SpaceX will first launch a depot ship to low Earth orbit (LEO) to serve as a fuel repository. The graphic indicates that multiple tanker Starships will dock with this depot to fill it, though the exact number of these initial flights is not specified.

Following the depot’s initial fill, the Starship lunar lander will launch to LEO to dock with the depot for its first fuel transfer. After undocking, the lander will raise its altitude to a designated "final tanking orbit" (FTO). At this stage, SpaceX will launch another round of multiple tanker ships to replenish the depot with additional propellant. The depot will then travel to the FTO to dock with the lander for a final fuel transfer before the lander ascends to high Earth orbit.

In high Earth orbit, the Starship lander will rendezvous and dock with NASA’s Orion capsule, which carries four astronauts launched aboard a Space Launch System (SLS) rocket. The combined spacecraft will burn their engines to travel toward the moon, separating upon arrival in low lunar orbit. Two astronauts will remain in Orion while the other two descend to the lunar surface in Starship. After their surface mission, the two astronauts will return to Starship, launch back to lunar orbit, and dock with Orion for the journey home.

NASA states that this complex sequence serves a specific purpose by creating flexibility in the launch schedule for the SLS rocket, which launches Orion before Starship completes its final fueling. The agency notes that this approach reduces the total fuel required compared to previous plans, primarily because Starship will take Orion directly to low lunar orbit rather than a much higher orbit.

Despite these detailed plans, the mission architecture is not finalized. NASA retains the option to select Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for Artemis IV if SpaceX fails to demonstrate its orbital refueling strategy or does not complete an uncrewed lunar landing mission by the end of next year. As the launch date approaches, further details regarding the specific number of refueling flights and the exact execution of the orbital maneuvers are expected to become clearer.
summary: Do we know how many Starship launches SpaceX will need to get NASA astronauts to the moon? No. Will its refuelling plan be simple? Also no.
author: Space.com

title: Astrobee robot cube assists astronauts on International Space Station
content:
A small robotic cube known as Astrobee is actively assisting astronauts aboard the International Space Station. NASA developed these free-flying robotic assistants to support mission operations in microgravity. The program began in 2019 with the arrival of the first two units, named Bumble and Honey. A third robot, named Queen, joined the station later that same year. Seven years after the initial deployment, the Astrobee program remains operational and effective.

The robots are designed to help astronauts test new technologies and allow mission teams on Earth to better observe the interior of the station. They also assist with everyday tasks for the crew. In a recent image taken by NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins, an Astrobee robot is shown operating within the station’s Kibo laboratory. The metal cubes are approximately the size of a toaster and move autonomously through the spacecraft.

The compact design and autonomous flight capabilities of Astrobee distinguish it from previous robotic systems in space. While not the first robot to operate on the space station, its form factor gives it a unique presence that resembles a companion to the crew. The continued success of the program raises questions about the future evolution of robotic assistants in space, including potential applications for lunar missions where robots might autonomously explore and aid astronauts.
summary: NASA's Astrobee robots are free-flying robotic assistants that help astronauts test new technologies and perform everyday chores in microgravity. The image shows one of the robots operating in the station's Kibo laboratory, a program that has been active since 2019.

title: On this day in space! Nov. 3, 1957: Laika the dog launches with Sputnik 2
content: On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth. Laika was a 3-year-old stray husky-spitz mix from the streets of Moscow, and she was recruited by the Soviet space program for her small size and calm temperament. Unfortunately for Laika, this mission was a one-way trip. The Soviets didn't design a way to bring her back down to Earth. With only 7 days worth of oxygen and a little bit of food on board, Laika launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan with a Russian Sputnik rocket. This was the same kind of rocket used to launch the first Sputnik satellite. Laika was alive when she reached orbit, but she died shortly afterward because the spacecraft's heat shield had broken off. Laika overheated before she had the chance to die of starvation of oxygen deprivation. Laika, the first Soviet space dog to enter Earth orbit, is seen in a training capsule prior to her launch. (Image credit: Roscosmos) Why it mattered Laika has remained one of space history's most beloved and tragic figures. People around the world have dogs as pets who they love as members of their own families. And even nearly 70 years after this flight, it is so heartbreaking to think of Laika on that frightening journey from which she never returned. Laika was one of many different animals that were used in early spaceflight testing. Both the U. S. And Russia launched a number of primates on flights testing early flight technology. Sadly, like Laika, many of these brave creatures did not make it back. Unbelievably, though, some did survive the journey. For example, the chimpanzee named Ham and nicknamed the "astrochimp" survived a 1961 test flight to space. Though, the team behind that flight was so unsure of how it would go that Ham didn't get his name until after it was found that he'd survived his return. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.
summary: On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth.
